title: IPC Section 420 / BNS – Bogus websites and cyber fraud
content: Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (now Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) – Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property. This section is widely applied to cyber fraud cases involving bogus websites, fake e-commerce portals, investment scam websites, phishing portals, and fraudulent online marketplaces. Punishment under IPC Section 420 is imprisonment up to 7 years with fine. In cybercrime cases, Section 420 IPC is typically read with relevant sections of the IT Act. The corresponding provision in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is Section 318. Victims of online fraud should file an FIR invoking these provisions along with IT Act sections and report at cybercrime.gov.in.

title: IPC Sections 463, 464, 468, 469 / BNS – E-mail spoofing and online forgery
content: Sections 463, 464, 468 and 469 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 as amended by the IT Act, 2000 to include electronic records and documents. Section 463 – Forgery: making a false document or electronic record with intent to cause damage or injury or to support any claim or title or to cause any person to part with property. Section 464 – Making a false document. Section 468 – Forgery for purpose of cheating, punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. Section 469 – Forgery for purpose of harming reputation, punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. E-mail spoofing, where the origin of a message is disguised, and creation of fraudulent electronic records are prosecuted under these sections read with the IT Act. After the IT Act amendment, electronic records and electronic documents are treated on par with physical documents for the purpose of these sections. Corresponding provisions exist in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

title: IPC Section 499 and 500 / BNS Section 356 – Online defamation
content: Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (now Section 356 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) – Defamation. Whoever by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person commits defamation. Online defamation through social media posts, WhatsApp forwards, YouTube videos, or blogs making false damaging allegations about a person are prosecutable. Creating fake profiles to defame, posting morphed images with defamatory intent, and making false allegations in viral posts are covered. Punishment under IPC Section 500 is simple imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.

title: IPC Section 503 and 506 / BNS Section 351 – Criminal intimidation by e-mail or online message
content: Section 503 defines criminal intimidation and Section 506 prescribes punishment under the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Now Section 351 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Sending threatening messages by e-mail, social media messages, WhatsApp, or any digital communication threatening to injure the person, reputation, or property of another with intent to cause alarm is criminal intimidation. Punishment for criminal intimidation is imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both. If the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, punishment extends to 7 years. Section 507 covers criminal intimidation by anonymous communication, which applies to threats sent from anonymous email accounts, fake social media profiles, and anonymous messaging platforms. Corresponding to BNS Section 351(3) and 351(4).

title: IPC Section 509 / BNS – Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman online
content: Section 509 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 – Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman. Whoever, intending to insult the modesty of any woman, utters any word, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits any object, intending that such word or sound shall be heard, or that such gesture or object shall be seen, by such woman, or intrudes upon the privacy of such woman, shall be punished with simple imprisonment up to 3 years, and also with fine. This section applies to online harassment of women including sending obscene messages, posting offensive comments targeting women on social media, intrusive messages through dating apps, and digital forms of sexual harassment. Read with IT Act Section 66E for privacy violations.

title: IPC Section 354D / BNS Section 77 – Cyberstalking
content: Section 354D of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (now Section 77 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) – Stalking. Any man who monitors the use by a woman of the internet, email, or any other form of electronic communication or watches or spies on a woman, commits the offence of stalking. Online or cyber stalking includes repeatedly sending messages despite clear indication of disinterest, tracking location via social media check-ins, monitoring a woman's online activity, and sending unwanted friend requests on social media platforms. Punishment on first offence is imprisonment up to 3 years with fine. On second or subsequent conviction, imprisonment up to 5 years with fine.

title: IPC Section 153A / BNS – Promoting enmity and hate speech online
content: Section 153A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 – Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc. and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony. Sharing content on social media platforms that promotes enmity between communities on the basis of religion, caste, race, or region is punishable under this section. Viral inflammatory social media posts, hate speech videos on YouTube, and communally charged messages forwarded on WhatsApp have been prosecuted under Section 153A. Punishment is imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both. If the offence is committed in a place of worship, punishment extends to 5 years with fine. The corresponding provision exists in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

title: IPC Section 383 / BNS – Web-jacking and cyber extortion
content: Section 383 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 – Extortion (Web-jacking). Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person, or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver any property or valuable security or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable security, commits extortion. Web-jacking involves taking over another person's website by hacking and demanding ransom for restoring access. Ransomware attacks where data is encrypted and ransom demanded are prosecuted under this section read with IT Act Section 66. Punishment for extortion under IPC is imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both, and up to 10 years in aggravated forms. The corresponding provision exists in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

title: IPC Sections 292, 292A, 293, 294 – Online obscenity and sale of obscene material
content: Sections 292, 292A, 293 and 294 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 – Obscenity provisions applicable to online content. Section 292 makes it an offence to sell, distribute, exhibit, or circulate any obscene book, pamphlet, paper, drawing, painting, representation or figure. Following the IT Act amendment, this includes electronic publications, websites, and digital material. Section 292A prohibits printing or publishing grossly indecent or scurrilous matter intended for blackmail. Section 293 prohibits sale of obscene objects to young persons. Section 294 prohibits obscene acts and songs. These sections complement IT Act Sections 67 and 67A for prosecution of online obscenity. Punishment ranges from imprisonment up to 2 to 3 years with fine. Corresponding provisions exist in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

title: IPC Sections 378, 379 – Theft of computer hardware
content: Sections 378 and 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 – Theft and punishment for theft. Section 378 defines theft as moving of moveable property with dishonest intention to take it out of the possession of any person without that person's consent. Section 379 prescribes punishment for theft up to 3 years or fine or both. Physical theft of computers, laptops, mobile phones, servers, hard drives, and other computer hardware containing confidential data is prosecuted under these sections. Such cases are often linked to IT Act offences if the stolen device contains sensitive personal or financial data. Corresponding provisions in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 apply.

title: Copyright Act Sections 51, 63, 63A, 63B – Software piracy and online copyright infringement
content: Sections 51, 63, 63A and 63B of the Copyright Act, 1957 – Online copyright infringement and software piracy. Section 51 defines when copyright is infringed including use of pirated software, unauthorised downloads, and streaming of copyrighted content. Section 63 prescribes the offence of infringement: any person who knowingly infringes or abets the infringement of copyright in a work is punishable with imprisonment from 6 months to 3 years and fine from Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh. Section 63A provides enhanced penalty on second and subsequent convictions. Section 63B makes knowing use of an infringing copy of a computer programme a specific criminal offence punishable with imprisonment from 7 days to 3 years and fine from Rs 50,000 to Rs 2 lakh. Software piracy, distribution of cracked software, and torrenting of copyrighted material are prosecuted under these provisions.

title: NDPS Act and Arms Act – Online sale of drugs and arms
content: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 and Arms Act, 1959 – Applied to online sale of drugs and illegal arms. Sale and purchase of narcotic drugs and controlled substances through online platforms, darknet markets, encrypted messaging apps, and social media channels is a serious offence under the NDPS Act with imprisonment ranging from 6 months to life imprisonment depending on the quantity, and fine up to Rs 2 lakh or more. Online sale and delivery of illegal weapons, firearms, and ammunition through e-commerce platforms or dark web markets violates the Arms Act and attracts imprisonment up to 3 years extendable to 7 years. These cases are typically investigated by the NCB (for drugs) and state police (for arms) in coordination with cyber cells, and charges include IT Act sections for computer-facilitated transactions.
